currentNews.title: The CVE Search API: A New Way to Access CVE Records

description.content: The CVE™ Program is introducing a new CVE Search API designed to make vulnerability information easier to find, easier to reuse, and easier to integrate into automated workflows. CVE Record information is already available for users through two channels: CVE List Search on the CVE website, and CVE List Downloads, the CVE Program’s bulk download capability on GitHub.

Both remain important parts of the CVE information distribution architecture. The new CVE Search API is intended to complement those capabilities by adding a modern, real-time, programmatic way to query the CVE List with precision.
Why a Search API Now?

As vulnerability reporting volumes continue to grow, so does the need for faster and more precise access to CVE data. Security teams, researchers, product vendors, and downstream integrations increasingly depend on automation to triage, enrich, and act on vulnerability information at scale. The new CVE Search API is being introduced to help meet that need. It is being designed to support precise searches across all CVE Record containers, enabling users to retrieve targeted vulnerability information quickly and accurately. Rather than replace existing access methods, it adds an important new option for users who need low-latency programmatic access to CVE data.

The CVE Program’s GitHub repository remains the right place for bulk access and download-oriented workflows. The cve.org website remains the primary interactive experience for browsing and discovering CVE Records as a human user. The new Search API adds a third capability for precise programmatic search through the API for automation and integration.

The technology behind the API has been built with long-term reliability and scalability in mind. This matters because many users are no longer just reading CVE information one record at a time. They are feeding it into dashboards, asset pipelines, prioritization tools, security analytics, and response processes. A dedicated API helps support that reality.
What Value a CVE Search API Will Bring

The CVE Program is committed to continually improving the quality, completeness, and efficient retrievability of the data available. The Search API is focused on making CVE information more usable in modern security operations and software workflows.
With this new capability, users are able to:

• Run repeatable searches from applications and automated processes
  • Combine filters such as weakness types, severity, exploitation indicators, dates, and other record attributes
  • Scope their searches across the multiple CVE Record containers with greater precision
  • Receive complete JSON CVE Records as result
Popular use cases may include:

• Searching for HIGH and CRITICAL in cvssV4Severity and cvssV3_1Severity
  • Searching for the principal SSVC fields (ssvcTechnicalImpact, ssvcAutomatable, and ssvcExploitation)
  • Searching by cweId (e.g., to find weakness examples)

Because of the limitations of data within CVE Records, not all of the documented search types currently provide data that is operationally viable. There will be fewer of these limitations in later iterations. It is also possible that, depending on community interest, the Search API will draw upon data elements contributed by organizations that partner with the CVE Program.
In practical terms, this means users are now able to move beyond simple keyword discovery and ask more focused questions of the CVE data they rely on every day.
Available Now: BETA Release and Practical Use

The BETA CVE Search API is being initially released as an open capability with no identification or authentication requirements. However, it includes service limits designed to support reliable and responsible use. The service returns complete CVE Records, along with documented paging behavior and explicit warnings where needed which will give integrators a clear, predictable contract for building against the API.
The BETA test period — scheduled to run October 13, 2026, through December 31, 2026 — is intended to give the community an opportunity to evaluate the capability.

Users are encouraged to begin experimenting with the API now, with the understanding that they are helping shape how it grows. Feedback on missing data, unexpected search behavior, or desired filters will directly inform the roadmap for enhancing both the technology and the completeness of the information it exposes.
Resources:

• CVE Search API Documentation (Swagger Docs)
  • CVE Search API Source Code (GitHub)
  • CVE Search API Feedback (Issue Tracker on GitHub)
Looking Ahead
The introduction of the CVE Search API reflects a broader goal of making high-quality CVE information easier to access, easier to search precisely, and easier to operationalize at scale.
In the near term, users should expect a series of enhancements and adjustments to the Search API behavior, as we review community feedback and deploy improvements rapidly.

As the vulnerability landscape grows more complex, the CVE ecosystem must continue to support both human users and automated systems. By complementing the GitHub repository and the cve.org website search experience, the new Search API is designed to strengthen the way CVE information is distributed and consumed across the global cybersecurity community — starting with a solid technical foundation today and evolving toward more complete and powerful data access tomorrow.

currentNews.title: CVE Program Data Registry: Automating Federated Management

description.content: Over the past decade, the CVE™ Program has expanded globally to include more than 550 collaborating organizations, with CVE Record publication increasingly federated across this community. Participation is expected to continue to expand. As this growth accelerates, the need to distribute management functions efficiently across program participants is more critical than ever.

The CVE Program “Data Registry” is designed to meet this need. The Data Registry is a web-based user interface and backing database that will ultimately enable CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs), Roots, Top-Level Roots to manage their own data (as well as the data of the organizations that they manage) more efficiently. It is a core component of the federation strategy, pushing day-to-day CVE Program management closer to the organizations doing the real work of publishing CVE Records.

This effort introduces and enhances two core capabilities: “Organizational Registry” functions and “User Registry” functions. Together, they reduce manual friction and give participating organizations greater agility and control.
Organizational Registry Functions

Organizational Registry functions allow participating organizations, such as CNAs, to provide and manage organizational information as they participate in the program. By moving away from manual queues, organizations gain direct control over their administrative profiles.
Key capabilities include:

• Efficient Onboarding: Streamlines the registration of new partner organizations and internal business units within the CVE community.
  • Self-Service Profile Updates: Enables organizations to immediately update key metadata, including legal names, primary contact information, and unique identifiers.
  • Parameter Auditing: Provides transparent visibility into an organization’s current scope, historical assignments, and publishing rights.
User Registry Functions
User Registry functions give precise control over who can interact with the CVE platforms on behalf of their organization.
Key capabilities include:

• Credential Lifecycle Control: Supports seamless provisioning, updating, and revocation of secure operational access credentials.
  • Role-Based Permissions: Defines clear user hierarchies, ensuring secure separation of duties between administrative managers and standard data publishers.
  • Immediate Status Management: Allows administrators to deactivate or reactivate user profiles instantly, supporting security and compliance during personnel changes.
Rollout Timeline

The initial rollout of the Registry is planned for October 2026 and will introduce a centrally accessible client for CNAs to manage their users and data. A subsequent deployment later in 2026 will expand capabilities to support Roots and Top-Level Roots.
Get Involved

The CVE Program Data Registry is an open-source CVE Program initiative. You can support and help shape this effort by joining the CVE Program Automation Working Group (AWG) or by reviewing the project materials (and offering feedback) available through the CVE Program’s CVE Services GitHub Repository.

currentNews.title: CNAs — Register Now for “CVE Program Fall Technical Workshop: Advancing CVE Record Quality” on October 29, 2026

description.content:
The CVE Program will host a “CVE Program Fall Technical Workshop: Advancing CVE Record Quality” virtual event for CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) on Thursday, October 29, 2026, from 10:00 AM – 4:00 PM EDT (UTC-4).

This CNA workshop is free, but registration is required. Information on how to register was sent directly to CNAs on September 3, with reminder emails sent on September 17 and October 5. Note that registration closes at 11:59 PM EDT on October 23, 2026.

The overall theme for this year’s workshop will be CVE Record Quality, but other topics important to CNAs will also be included. As in years past, the Fall Technical Workshop is designed for CNAs, and will provide opportunities to engage on a wide range of CVE Program technical topics.

Agenda topics are expected to include:
  • CNA practices – how do you define, measure, and improve the quality of your CVE Records
  • Vulnerability management tooling – how your tools use, enrich, normalize, or interpret CVE Record data
  • Downstream consumers – what information do enterprise users need from CVE Records, and where do quality gaps create challenges
  • CNA Rules – updates and clarifications
  • CVE Program Policies – updates and clarifications
  • CVE Services - Data Registry demonstration
  • CVE and AI vulnerability discovery – follow-on discussions
Registration

Registration is open until 11:59 PM EDT on October 23, 2026.

Details were sent to CNAs by email on September 3, 2026, with reminder emails sent on September 17, 2026, and October 5, 2026.
All CNAs should attend this workshop. There is no limit on the number of attendees that can participate from your organization.

currentNews.title: Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records: 281 CNAs on the Enrichment Recognition List for October 5, 2026

description.altText: Increasing the Value of the CVE Record - CNA Enrichment Recognition List

description.content: The “CNA Enrichment Recognition List” for October 5, 2026, is now available with 281 CNAs listed. Published monthly on the CVE website, the list recognizes those CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) that are actively providing enhanced vulnerability data in their CVE Records. CNAs are added to the list if they provide Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) in at least 98% of their records that were published within two weeks of their most recently published record.

CNA Enrichment Recognition List criteria and reporting are intended to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same. Enrichment Recognition List criteria may change over time. The most recent modifications occurred in June 2025 when data pulls were moved from every two weeks and based upon data from the last 12 months, to the current reporting of once-per-month data pulls based upon data from the previous six months.

For more about the recognition list, see “Recognition for CNAs Actively Providing Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records.” To learn more about vulnerability information types like CVSS and CWE, see the CVE Record User Guide. View the most current CNA Enrichment Recognition List on the CVE website Metrics page here.

currentNews.title: The CVE Program’s Quality Era: Modernizing the CVE Program Automation Support System

description.content: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) recent “CVE Program: Establishing a Quality Era Framework,” white paper describes how the CVE™ Program is evolving to keep pace with a rapidly changing vulnerability landscape. That publication introduced the four major dimensions of quality and outlined CISA’s strategic lines of effort for a “Quality Era” focused on reliability, responsiveness, and better vulnerability data.

This blog is the first in an infrastructure-focused series of blogs where we will take a closer look at how the CVE Program is modernizing the technology and automation that sit behind CVE Identifier (CVE ID) reservation and CVE Records creation and publication.
Why Infrastructure Modernization, and Why Now

The vulnerability ecosystem has shifted from manual, linear workflows to highly automated, parallel processes. Modern tooling, continuous integration pipelines, automated scanners, and AI-assisted research can all surface vulnerabilities at once — and often from multiple sources.

This acceleration brings concrete operational pressures:
  • Higher volumes of submissions arriving in shorter timeframes
  • More overlapping or duplicate reports from different reporters
  • Shorter expectations for coordinated disclosure and publication
  • More demand for structured, machine-readable CVE data

The CVE Program’s core mission — providing unique identifiers and consistent, public vulnerability records — has not changed. What is changing is the infrastructure that enables the Program to carry out that mission reliably on a global scale.

As highlighted in the Quality Era framework, data infrastructure is one of the key dimensions of program quality. Modernizing that infrastructure is essential to:
  • Keep pace with current and projected CVE volumes
  • Embed validation and quality checks earlier in the process
  • Support a broader, more diverse set of CNAs, Roots, CNAs of Last Resort (CNA-LR)
  • Improve how downstream tools and services consume CVE data

This blog outlines several automation and infrastructure efforts that are either underway or being explored. Future posts in this series will go deeper into technical details, implementation timelines, and opportunities for community feedback.

While the CVE Program has been adding automation and infrastructure improvements for some time, new enhancements are now underway. Beginning in Fall 2026, the CVE Program will be investing in several new foundational automation and infrastructure capabilities.
Enhanced CVE Services and Validation Library

The “CVE Services Validation Library” is an independent library that CVE Services will integrate to apply consistent checks when users submit CVE Records for publication. Because it is independent, any CVE application can adopt it, allowing record creators around the world to use the same validation logic that supports the official publication process.

Over time, this validation library is expected to evolve alongside the CVE Record Format and quality criteria, giving the program a more agile way to improve data quality without requiring each CNA to build and maintain their own custom checks.
CVE Program Data Registry

The “CVE Program Data Registry” is a modern registry for managing identity, organizational metadata, and role information for CVE partners and contributors, including CNAs, Roots, CNA-LRs, and other participants.
It will provide more accurate and timely information about who is participating and in what capacity, as well as greater control over user and role management for participating organizations.

By improving how the program models and manages its own community, the Data Registry supports both governance and infrastructure quality goals, while making day-to-day participation more efficient for CNAs and Roots.
CVE Reference Archive (Exploratory)

The “CVE Reference Archive” is a proposed capability to preserve referenced content — such as advisories, vendor writeups, or guidance documents — or to store stable representations of that content as it existed near the time of CVE publication. It attempts to address link rot and broken references that accumulate over time when webpages, files, or websites are moved or are no longer accessible.

If implemented, a CVE Reference Archive would not replace primary sources but would provide a fallback so users can maintain confidence that references cited in CVE Records remain accessible and verifiable over the long term.

The CVE reference archive capability raises important legal, operational, and technical questions. Because of this, it remains an exploratory effort. Community input will be critical to determining scope, governance, and feasibility.
CVE Repository Search API (Exploratory)

The CVE Program currently has a Search Capability on its home page. This effort will explore the viability of a “Search Application Programming Interface (API)” that supports a more flexible, machine-based search and filtering capability to augment the basic search capability that currently exists.
This initiative is in an exploratory phase. Feedback from downstream users will help prioritize features, performance requirements, and governance expectations.
What’s Next

Modernizing infrastructure alone does not deliver quality, but it is a necessary foundation. These efforts are intended to make it easier for the CVE community to apply shared policies, adhere to consistent quality expectations, and deliver timely, actionable records at scale.
As these initiatives mature, the CVE Program will continue to work through the AWG and the comments from the public to gather feedback and refine priorities.
How to Get Involved

The success of the Quality Era depends on active participation from the global cybersecurity community. If you operate as a CNA, Root, or CNA-LR, maintain tools or rely on CVE Records for vulnerability management, research, or policy work we encourage you to share your needs and experiences.
To learn more about these efforts and provide input on the exploratory initiatives, join the CVE Program Automation Working Group (AWG) and make your voice heard.

Together, the vulnerability management community can ensure that the CVE Program’s infrastructure remains resilient, transparent, and ready for a high-volume, AI-accelerated future — while preserving its role as a trusted public good.

currentNews.title: CISA Releases White Paper “CVE Program: Establishing a Quality Era Framework”

description.content: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has released a new white paper, “CVE Program: Establishing a Quality Era Framework,” describing the next phase of CVE™ Program maturation. As the CVE ecosystem continues to expand globally and vulnerability volumes rise, the paper emphasizes a renewed focus on reliability, responsiveness, and vulnerability data quality.

The white paper explains that the CVE Program is moving beyond a period of growth into a “Quality Era” shaped by increasing demand, higher submission volumes, and new pressures introduced by automation and AI-enabled technologies.
Rather than treating quality as a single technical issue, CISA describes it as a program-wide effort spanning four connected dimensions:

• Program Governance
  • Ecosystem Participation
  • Data Infrastructure
  • CVE Record Content
The white paper also maps these quality dimensions to six strategic lines of effort:

• Expand on Community Partnerships
  • Government Sponsorship
  • Modernization, Transparency, and Communication
  • Data Quality Improvements
  • Improvements in CNA of Last Resort (CNA-LR)
Together, these workstreams are intended to strengthen the resilience, consistency, and usability of the CVE Program across the global vulnerability management community.

CISA also notes that future Quality Era publications will provide more detail on specific initiatives, including upcoming blog posts on cve.org covering technology, infrastructure, and data modernization efforts that support quality at scale.

currentNews.title: CVE Podcast — CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) Scopes

description.content:
In this episode of the “We Speak CVE” podcast, podcast host Shannon Sabens chats with Alicia Mink of the MITRE Top-Level Root and Julia Turkevich of the CISA Top-Level Root about CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scopes.

Within the CVE Program, the term “scope” refers to the set of products, projects, services, organizations, constituencies, or cases for which a CNA is authorized to assign CVE IDs and publish CVE Records. A well-written CNA scope sets expectations, helps manage workload, improves coordination across the CVE ecosystem, and gives vulnerability reporters a clearer path to the right authority.

Topics discussed in this episode include how to write a scope, how the type of CNA organization (vendor, researcher, open source, CERT, hosted service, bug bounty provider, and/or consortium organization) influence what’s included in a scope, ensuring the scope aligns to the CNA Operational Rules, avoiding scope overlap, end-of-life (EOL) products, extended-support products, how scopes might evolve over time, and more.

Resources mentioned in the podcast include:
  • CNA Scope Examples (List of Partners page)
  • CNA Operational Rules
  • CVE Program EOL Policy
  • How to Become a CNA Partner

“We Speak CVE” is a free podcast about cybersecurity, vulnerability management, and the CVE Program. Listen on the CVE Program Channel on YouTube, on We Speak CVE page on Buzzsprout, and on major podcast directories such as Spotify, Stitcher, Apple Podcasts, iHeartRadio, Podcast Addict, Podchaser, Pocket Casts, Deezer, Listen Notes, Player FM, and Podcast Index, among others.

description.content:
The CVE Program will host a “CVE Program Fall Technical Workshop: Advancing CVE Record Quality” virtual event for CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) on Thursday, October 29, 2026, from 10:00 AM – 4:00 PM EDT (UTC-4).

Published monthly on the CVE website, the list recognizes those CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) that are actively providing enhanced vulnerability data in their CVE Records. CNAs are added to the list if they provide Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) in at least 98% of their records that were published within two weeks of their most recently published record.

CNA Enrichment Recognition List criteria and reporting are intended to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same. currentNews.title: “CNA Rules v4.2.0” Now in Effect

description.content: The CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) Operational Rules Version 4.2.0 took effect on August 25, 2026, after community input and review. The previous version, CNA Rules v4.1.0, has been deprecated. CNAs are now required to comply with the CNA Rules v4.2.0.

CNA Rules v4.2.0, which was updated to improve the clarity of the rules, was approved by the CVE Board on August 20, 2026. A detailed report is available that lists all changes between Version 4.1.0 and Version 4.2.0.
Changes for CNA Rules v4.2.0 include, but are not limited to, the following:

• Updated section 3.2.4.2 to require the CVE ID assignment request method free from restrictive disclosure terms
  • Changed section 4.1.3 to add additional guidance for determining insecure default configuration vulnerabilities
  • Changed section 4.1.6 to clarify detection and exploit mitigation bypass
  • Changed section 4.2.1.3 to clarify that dispute resolution is not needed when parties agree about vulnerability determination
  • Relocated text regarding detect and resolve multiple assignment requests from section 4.2.19-20 to section 4.2.16.7-8
  • Updated section 4.2.16.9 to include instructions to coordinate assignments for Publicly Disclosed vulnerabilities with other CNAs and CNA-LRs
  • Updated section 5.1.7.1 to temporarily allow missing type or cause of vulnerability
  • Typographical fixes and re-numbering
  • Added a Revision History section to CNA Rules document
The CNA Rules v4.2.0 is available now on the CVE website as a PDF (0.2MB) and on the CNA Rules web page.

currentNews.title: Meeting Notes from “CVE and AI Vulnerability Discovery” Virtual Conference Now Available
currentNews.urlKeywords: CVE AI Vulnerability Discovery Conference Meeting Notes

description.content: Meeting notes are now available from “CVE in an Era of AI-Enabled Vulnerability Discovery,” a free public virtual conference hosted by the CVE™ Program on July 30, 2026. The purpose of the conference was to open a CVE community discussion about AI-enabled vulnerability discovery. The conference was presented as both a listening forum and a working forum, with the explicit goal of surfacing pressure points, practical responses, and areas where follow-up work may be needed rather than announcing a predetermined policy outcome.
Meeting notes from the conference are available here.
A video of the conference is also available on the CVE Program Channel on YouTube.
Key Conference Takeaways
An overview of the key takeaways from the conference, each of which is described in more detail in the meeting notes, is below.

• AI Is Increasing Pressure Across the Vulnerability Lifecycle – Higher report volumes are increasing workload across triage, validation, remediation, CVE assignment, and downstream vulnerability management.
  • Prioritization Matters More as Volume Grows – Participants emphasized that more vulnerabilities do not automatically mean greater risk. Exploitability, exposure, and organizational context are increasingly important for determining which vulnerabilities require action.
  • Quality and Validation Must Keep Pace – False positives, duplicate findings, hallucinations, and uneven report quality are creating additional work. AI can help scale triage and record development, but human verification remains important.
  • Remediation and Automation Need Greater Investment – Participants stressed that discovery must be matched by the ability to fix vulnerabilities at scale. Automation, stronger remediation workflows, and better tooling were viewed as necessary responses to increasing volume.
  • Open-Source Maintainers Need More Support – Resource-constrained maintainers are absorbing significant additional workload. Participants called for greater funding, expertise, patches, and tooling from organizations that depend on open-source software.
  • CVE Data and Processes Need Continued Improvement – Participants identified gaps in product mapping, identifiers, enrichment, assignment, and interoperability that limit automation and create downstream confusion. Discussion supported further work on data standards and CVE processes but did not produce clear consensus on the scope of broader program changes.
  • Education and Engagement – As an undercurrent to the primary discussion themes, many participants among both speakers and listeners pointed to a sustained need for increased engagement throughout the CVE community to share knowledge and enhance.
The full meeting notes are available as a PDF on the Resources page CVE website.
Attendee Survey
A post-conference survey will be sent by email sent to all attendees. Thank you in advance for completing the survey. Your responses will help us shape future CVE Program events on this topic.

description.content: The CVE Program’s quarterly summary of program milestones and metrics for Q2 CY 2026.
Q2 CY 2026 Milestones
Twenty-Five CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) Added
The twenty-five (25) new CNAs added this quarter are listed below under their Top-Level Root (TL-Root) or Root. Scope of coverage is described next to their organization name.

  • Eclypsium, Inc. – All software created and distributed by Eclypsium, as well as vulnerabilities discovered by, or reported to, Eclypsium that are not in another CNA’s scope. (USA)
  • Entrust Corporation – All products under the following brand names: Entrust, Datacard, Entrust Datacard, nCipher, Onfido, Hytrust, SafeLayer, Antelop, Evidos, SMS Passcode. (USA)

(Luxembourg)
  • GVision Italia S.r.l. – Vulnerabilities affecting EU-certified and EU-hardened firmware, software components, and related services distributed and maintained by GVision Italia.   • IQSIGHT B.V. – All IQSIGHT (formerly Bosch Building Technology - Video Systems) products including end-of-life products. (Netherlands)
  • Orange Cyberdefense – Orange Cyberdefense branded products and technologies, unless embedded component or software covered by the scope of another CNA; as well as vulnerabilities in third-party software discovered by Orange Cyberdefense that are not in another CNA’s scope. (France)
  • VulNow – Vulnerabilities observed by, discovered by, or reported to VulNow that are not in another CNA’s scope. (Netherlands)
  • Ygreky SASU – All Ygreky products and infrastructure, and vulnerabilities discovered by, or reported to, Ygreky that are not covered by the scope of another CNA. (France)

(USA)

CVE Program Announces a “CVE and AI Vulnerability Discovery” Virtual Conference Will Be Held on July 30

In June, the community was informed that the upcoming “CVE and AI Vulnerability Discovery” virtual conference would be held on July 30, 2026. The conference was first announced on June 15 in the “CVE in an Era of AI-Enabled Vulnerability Discovery: Opening a Community Discussion — A Free Virtual Conference” blog article. The blog explained that the purpose of the event would be to open a structured community discussion about how AI-enabled vulnerability discovery is affecting the CVE Program and the broader vulnerability management ecosystem — and where current models may need to adapt. Community members were also asked to save the date for the conference. A second blog announcing that registration for the conference was open and asking for the community to submit discussion topics for the conference agenda was published on June 30. Additional blogs were published in July leading up to the event.
Preserving Vulnerability-Level Identification in a Time of Increased Disclosure Volume

One June 16, the CVE Program published the Preserving Vulnerability-Level Identification in a Time of Increased Disclosure Volume blog article recognizing that vulnerability disclosure is under real and growing pressure because the volume and velocity of vulnerability discovery are increasing, and AI-assisted research, automation, and large-scale analysis are changing the pace at which vulnerabilities are found, reported, triaged, remediated, and published. Some in the community have responded by bundling multiple different vulnerabilities under a single CVE ID, but the blog emphasizes that the CVE Program does not support assigning a single CVE ID to multiple distinct vulnerabilities when those vulnerabilities are independently understandable, independently exploitable, independently fixable, or independently relevant to defenders. The blog further stated that the CVE Program is committed to working with the community on scalable approaches that preserve vulnerability-level specificity and has scheduled a “CVE and AI Vulnerability Discovery” event for July 30 to open that discussion.
Ongoing Recognition for CNAs Actively Providing Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records

The CVE Program publicly recognizes those CNAs that are actively providing enhanced vulnerability data in their CVE Records. The “CNA Enrichment Recognition List,” published monthly, recognizes CNAs that provide Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) information based upon a monthly data pull of the previous six months.

The recognition list was published on June 1 with 259 CNAs recognized, May 4 with 261 CNAs recognized, and April 6 with 258 CNAs recognized.

CNA Enrichment Recognition List criteria and reporting are intended to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same. Enrichment Recognition List criteria may change over time. The most recent modifications occurred in June 2025 when data pulls were moved from every two weeks and based upon data from the last 12 months, to the current reporting of once-per-month data pulls based upon data from the previous six months. Future changes to the ERL qualification criteria and reporting may occur over time as the CVE Program continually aims to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same.
Supplier CNA as Authorized Data Publisher Pilot (SADP Pilot) Progressed in Production and Expanded

In May, the CVE™ Program announced that content from the “Supplier CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) as Authorized Data Publisher Pilot (SADP Pilot)” was now live in published CVE Records. SADP Pilot participants (Cisco, HeroDevs, Microsoft, Oracle, Red Hat, and Siemens) can add SADP (i.e., VEX-like) content to CVE Records as data points on how reported vulnerabilities affect their products. All SADP-enriched records are viewable on the official CVE List and through a dedicated SADP GitHub repository, which is synchronized with the official CVE List repository every 15 minutes.

In June, the Program announced that phase one of the pilot had been successful, with initial Supplier CNA ADP Siemens publishing over 800 enriched SADP records. The pilot was also expanded to invite additional Supplier CNAs and more downstream users to participate, and the timeframe—originally scheduled to conclude in July 2026—was extended to support additional testing and feedback.
Yogesh Mittal of Red Hat Joins CVE Board

In June, the CVE Program welcomed Yogesh Mittal of Red Hat as the newest member of the CVE Board. Yogesh brings nearly 20 years of experience to the Board, offering a perspective that bridges the gap between enterprise vulnerability consumers and open-source suppliers. Yogesh has made significant contributions to the CVE Program over the years, including helping Red Hat become a CVE Program Root, overseeing the onboarding of over 17 CNAs under the Red Hat Root, helping the Red Hat Root achieve CNA of Last Resort (CNA-LR) designation for its Root hierarchy, and representing the Red Hat Root on the Council of Roots (CoR).
New and Improved “CVE Program Web Forms” Now Available

In May, the CVE Program announced that new and improved versions of the “CVE Program Web Forms” were now available for use by the community. The forms include General Support (formerly “Other”), CVE ID Requests (from MITRE CNA-LR only), Report a Reserved by Public CVE ID, Join a Working Group, Register to Become a CNA, and more. Once a request is submitted using the new forms, requesters receive a ticket number and can see responses in the web form portal. An email message is also sent when a response to the request is posted in the portal. The CVE Program Web Forms are to be used for all inquiries to the CVE Program Secretariat and to request CVE IDs from the MITRE CNA of Last Resort (MITRE CNA-LR).

Metrics for Q2 CY 2026 Published CVE Records and Reserved CVE IDs are included below. Annual metrics are also included in the charts for year-to-year comparisons.

Terminology
  • Published: When a CNA populates the data associated with a CVE ID as a CVE Record, the state of the CVE Record is Published. The associated data must contain an identification number (CVE ID), a prose description, and at least one public reference.
  • Reserved: The initial state for a CVE Record; when the associated CVE ID is Reserved by a CNA.

description.content: CNA Partners Grow the CVE List
All of the CVE IDs and CVE Records cited in the metrics above are assigned and published by CNAs and the three CNA-LRs, within their own specific scopes.

CNAs partner with the program from a variety of business sectors; there are minimal requirements, and there is no monetary fee or contract to sign. Currently, 543 organizations (540 CNAs and 3 CNA-LRs) from 43 countries and 1 no country affiliation are partners with the CVE Program.
Learn how to become a CNA or contact one of the following to start the partnering process today:

• CISA Top-Level Root: Vulnerabilities that are (1) reported to or observed by CISA and (2) affect critical infrastructure, U.S. civilian government, industrial control systems, or medical devices, and (3) are not covered by another CNA’s scope
    • CERT@VDE Root: Organizations that are cooperative partners of CERT@VDE
    • CISA ICS Root: Vulnerabilities that are (1) reported to or observed by CISA, (2) affect industrial control systems or medical devices, and (3) are not covered by another CNA’s scope
  • MITRE Top-Level Root: Vulnerabilities, and Open-Source software product vulnerabilities, not already covered by a CNA listed on this website
    • ENISA Root: European Union (EU) member states/EU authorities, EU CSIRTs network members, and cooperative partners under ENISA’s mandate as well as other CNAs who choose ENISA as their Root
    • Google Root: Alphabet organizations
    • INCIBE Root: Spain organizations
    • JPCERT/CC Root: Japan organizations
    • Red Hat Root: The Red Hat Root’s scope includes the open-source community. Any open-source organizations that prefer Red Hat as their Root; organizations are free to choose another Root if it suits them better
    • Thales Group Root: Products and technologies of subsidiaries of Thales Group

currentNews.title: CVE Program Launches Frontier AI Researcher CNA Pilot
currentNews.urlKeywords: CVE Launches Frontier AI Researcher CNA Pilot

description.content:
Today, the CVE™ Program is launching the Frontier AI Researcher CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) Pilot, an initial six-month effort with Anthropic and OpenAI. This is a closed pilot, and participation is limited at this time to these two organizations. The pilot is intended to help the CVE Program evaluate how the large-scale, AI-enabled vulnerability research capabilities of frontier AI labs can contribute to accurate, coordinated, actionable, and sustainable CVE Records.

Under the pilot, Anthropic and OpenAI may assign CVE Identifiers (CVE IDs) for vulnerabilities they discover in widely adopted products and applications when those products are not already within another CNA’s scope.

This pilot supplements and does not replace, waive, or modify the CNA Operational Rules; participating organizations remain responsible for complying with all applicable CNA requirements. The effort is deliberately focused on products and applications that have achieved meaningful adoption, deployment, or ecosystem significance. The CVE Program is not accepting additional pilot participants at this time. At the end of the initial six-month period, the CVE Program will review the pilot’s outcomes, risks, operational burden, and value to CVE consumers before determining whether to continue, modify, expand, extend, or conclude the effort.
Additional Information
Additional information about the pilot’s purpose, scope, operating requirements, and evaluation approach is available in the Frontier AI Researcher CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) Pilot document.
Feedback Requested
A Frontier AI Researcher CNAs Pilot repository is also available on GitHub. Please use the repository Issue Tracker to provide feedback.
Ongoing community feedback will help inform whether the participating CNAs should retain this researcher scope beyond the evaluation period.
Note: This blog article was updated on August 20, 2026, to add the feedback information.

description.altText: Increasing the Value of the CVE Record - CNA Enrichment Recognition List

description.content: The “CNA Enrichment Recognition List” for July 6, 2026, is now available with 268 CNAs listed. Published monthly on the CVE website, the list recognizes those CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) that are actively providing enhanced vulnerability data in their CVE Records. CNAs are added to the list if they provide Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) in at least 98% of their records that were published within two weeks of their most recently published record.

CNA Enrichment Recognition List criteria and reporting are intended to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same. Enrichment Recognition List criteria may change over time. The most recent modifications occurred in June 2025 when data pulls were moved from every two weeks and based upon data from the last 12 months, to the current reporting of once-per-month data pulls based upon data from the previous six months.

For more about the recognition list, see “Recognition for CNAs Actively Providing Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records.” To learn more about vulnerability information types like CVSS and CWE, see the CVE Record User Guide. currentNews.title: Lindsey Cerkovnik of CISA Joins the CVE Board as the “CISA CVE Board Liaison”
currentNews.urlKeywords: Lindsey Cerkovnik CISA CVE Board Liaison

description.content: The CVE Program is pleased to announce that Lindsey Cerkovnik of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is the newest member of the CVE Board, serving as the “CISA CVE Board Liaison.”

description.altText: Lindsey Cerkovnik, CISA Liaison to the CVE Board
description.captionText:
Lindsey Cerkovnik –
CISA Liaison to the CVE Board

description.content: Per the CVE Board Charter, “Section 1.3.3 Organizational Liaison – An Organizational Liaison position allows for tighter partnerships with targeted organizations. This type of role provides the Board with greater flexibility for how external organizations work with the Board and CVE Program governance. There can be one or more organization(s) designated to have a liaison relationship with the Board at any one time. Each Organization with a Liaison position will have a single seat on the Board reserved for the Organizational Liaison representing them. This allows the Board representation from specific organizations as needed. This is a term-limited seat that must be reconfirmed by the Secretariat when the term set expires. The default term, unless specified by the Board during the establishment of the organization’s liaison role, is one year. The Secretariat assures the Organization wishes to continue the Board relationship and that the designated individual is the proper person to fill the role for the organization for the upcoming term. The Organization’s liaison is a voting member of the Board and can serve more than one consecutive term if the Organization desires. This position is a two-way conduit for the Organization to bring things to and from the Board in an official and structured way.”
About Lindsey Cerkovnik

Lindsey Cerkovnik serves as the Chief for the Vulnerability Response and Coordination (VRC) at CISA. In this role, she leads the teams responsible for CISA’s Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) process, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, and vulnerability prioritization efforts that serve as the foundation for U.S. federal, civilian, executive branch agencies’ vulnerability response efforts.

Lindsey and her team help to maintain, support, and advance the global vulnerability ecosystem by sponsoring, overseeing, and participating in the CVE and CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) programs, leading the production and dissemination of machine-readable vulnerability information, and engaging in valuable technical collaboration with the vulnerability research community. Through their work analyzing, triaging, and disclosing hundreds of thousands of vulnerabilities, they understand the value of prioritization, automation, and scalability for a growing and changing technology world.

Prior to her work at CISA, Lindsey conducted cybersecurity investigations with a focus on digital forensics in support of national security. She also conducted intelligence analysis and research and development related to industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) cybersecurity, energy infrastructure supply chains, ICS/OT vulnerability discovery and disclosure, and software development and testing.
About the CVE Board

Through open and collaborative discussions, the CVE Board helps ensure that the CVE Program meets the vulnerability identification needs of the global cybersecurity and technology communities. Board members represent numerous cybersecurity-related organizations, including commercial security tool vendors, academia, research institutions, government departments and agencies, and other prominent security experts, as well as end-users of vulnerability information.

currentNews.title: Yogesh Mittal of Red Hat Joins CVE Board
currentNews.urlKeywords: Yogesh Mittal Red Hat CVE Board

description.content: The CVE Program is pleased to welcome Yogesh Mittal of Red Hat as the newest member of the CVE Board. Yogesh brings nearly 20 years of experience to the CVE Board, offering a unique perspective that bridges the gap between enterprise vulnerability consumers and open-source suppliers.

description.altText: CVE Board Member Yogesh Mittal
description.captionText: CVE Board Member Yogesh Mittal

description.content: About Yogesh

Yogesh is the Manager of Red Hat Product Security. In this role, he manages a global team responsible for executing end-to-end Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) operations for Red Hat’s extensive enterprise portfolio as well as upstream community projects.

Having joined Red Hat in 2020, his role highlights the structural challenges and burnout experienced by unfunded open-source maintainers, while his broader industry background exposed him to the “triage drain” enterprise security teams face when chasing down vulnerabilities.

Yogesh has made significant contributions to the CVE Program over the years, including spearheading the strategic initiative for Red Hat to become a CVE Program Root, overseeing the successful onboarding of over 17+ CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) under the Red Hat Root, and leading the effort for the Red Hat Root to achieve the CNA of Last Resort (CNA-LR) designation for its Root hierarchy. Yogesh also represents the Red Hat Root on the Council of Roots (CoR), bringing a vital open-source perspective to the group.
About the CVE Board

currentNews.title: Preserving Vulnerability-Level Identification in a Time of Increased Disclosure Volume

description.content: Key Takeaway: The CVE Program does not support assigning a single CVE ID to multiple distinct vulnerabilities when those vulnerabilities are independently understandable, independently exploitable, independently fixable, or independently relevant to defenders. The CVE Program is committed to working with the community on scalable approaches that preserve vulnerability-level specificity.
Introduction

The CVE™ Program recognizes that vulnerability disclosure is under real and growing pressure. The volume and velocity of vulnerability discovery are increasing, and AI-assisted research, automation, and large-scale analysis are changing the pace at which vulnerabilities are found, reported, triaged, remediated, and published.

As part of the CVE Program’s broader discussion on AI-enabled vulnerability discovery and scale, including the upcoming CVE Program community event on July 30, 2026, this post addresses one specific risk: preserving vulnerability-level identification.

The CVE Program is ready to work with CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs), Roots, vendors, researchers, PSIRTs, vulnerability management teams, tooling providers, data consumers, and downstream defenders on practical ways to scale. The community needs both near-term improvements and longer-term solutions. But as new approaches are considered, one principle must remain clear:

A CVE ID identifies a publicly disclosed vulnerability. It is not a patch name, advisory name, release name, or bucket for groups of distinct issues.

The mission of the CVE Program is to identify, define, and catalog publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities. That vulnerability-level specificity is not incidental. It is the foundation that allows the global defensive community to speak a common language about risk, exploitation, remediation, impact, and ecosystem-wide coordination.
Bundling Distinct Vulnerabilities Undermines the Purpose of CVE

The CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) Operational Rules state:

4.2.6 CNAs SHOULD assign different CVE IDs to separate Vulnerabilities, as determined using the guidance in 4.1.

Yet, recent discussions across the vulnerability disclosure community have raised the possibility of assigning a single CVE ID to multiple distinct vulnerabilities, sometimes grouped by product release, patch, code area, weakness category, or remediation vehicle.

The CVE Program does not support assigning a single CVE ID to multiple distinct vulnerabilities when those vulnerabilities are independently understandable, independently exploitable, independently fixable, or independently relevant to defenders.

Bundling multiple distinct vulnerabilities under one CVE ID changes the nature of the CVE Program. It moves CVE away from being a vulnerability identification system and toward becoming a patch naming or advisory grouping system. That shift would have significant consequences for the entire defensive ecosystem.

A software update may remediate many vulnerabilities. An advisory may describe many vulnerabilities. A coordinated release may include many fixes. But the CVE IDs associated with those fixes must continue to identify the underlying vulnerabilities, not merely the release vehicle used to deliver remediation.

The community should distinguish between batching disclosure and bundling identification. Coordinating release dates, publishing multiple CVE Records together, aligning advisories, or improving automation may help organizations manage increased volume while preserving vulnerability-level specificity.
Why This Matters to Defenders

CVE IDs are used far beyond disclosure notices. They are embedded throughout the cybersecurity ecosystem as durable, machine-readable, widely understood identifiers. Security teams use them to prioritize remediation. Product security teams use them to coordinate disclosure. Researchers use them to connect technical analysis across sources. Vulnerability intelligence providers use them to enrich records. Data scientists use them to study trends. Governments and critical infrastructure operators use them to understand exposure and risk.
When multiple distinct vulnerabilities are collapsed into one identifier, that ecosystem loses precision.

Bundling can make it harder to determine:
  • which specific vulnerability is being exploited
  • which vulnerability has a proof of concept
  • which products, versions, configurations, or components are affected
  • which vulnerability has been remediated by a given patch
  • which issue should be prioritized based on severity, exploitability, exposure, or asset criticality
  • which vulnerability intelligence, detection logic, or mitigation guidance applies
  • how to correlate vulnerability data across scanners, SBOM/VEX workflows, advisories, exploit databases, incident reports, and telemetry
  • how to perform reliable trend analysis, metrics, and machine-learning research over time
This loss of specificity does not reduce risk for defenders. It shifts complexity downstream.

A bundled identifier may appear simpler at the point of publication, but it creates ambiguity for every user who must interpret, enrich, prioritize, detect, or act on the information afterward. Defenders need more clarity as vulnerability volume increases, not less.
A Call to CNAs and the Broader Community
The CVE Program asks CNAs not to bundle distinct vulnerabilities under a single CVE ID when those vulnerabilities should be identified separately.

The CVE Program continues to seek and value input from across the vulnerability community. We recognize that increased volume, AI-assisted discovery, and changing disclosure practices may require thoughtful changes to existing processes. Those changes should be collaborative, evidence-based, and fit for purpose, while preserving the vulnerability-level specificity that downstream users require.

We also invite community stakeholders to work with the CVE Program on practical ways to address increased volume. The community needs both short-term improvements and long-term solutions. Those solutions may include better tooling, clearer guidance, improved automation, more scalable reservation and publication workflows, enhanced enrichment, and updated practices for managing high-volume disclosures.

As part of the CVE Program’s broader community discussion on AI-enabled vulnerability discovery and scale, we encourage stakeholders to bring their perspectives to the upcoming July 30, 2026, virtual community event — “CVE in an Era of AI-Enabled Vulnerability Discovery” — and related feedback channels. Input on high-volume disclosure workflows, CVE Record quality, downstream correlation, vulnerability enrichment, and the impacts of bundled identifiers will help inform practical next steps.

The CVE Program is committed to working with the community on these issues. We want to understand the operational pressures CNAs are facing, the needs of downstream users, and the ways current processes can be improved. We also welcome feedback on where existing guidance may need clarification.

But the central principle must remain intact:

A CVE ID should identify a publicly disclosed vulnerability.
Preserving that principle is essential to the CVE Program’s mission and to the defenders, researchers, data scientists, vendors, governments, and users who rely on CVE every day.

currentNews.title: “Supplier ADP Pilot Update” — Additional Supplier CNA Participants Wanted!
currentNews.urlKeywords: SADP Pilot Additional CNA Participants Wanted

description.content: The CVE™ Program’s “Supplier CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) as Authorized Data Publisher Pilot (SADP Pilot)” has been up and running in production since April 2026.

Phase one of the pilot has been successful, with initial Supplier CNA ADP Siemens publishing over 800 enriched SADP records. These CVE Records provide the cybersecurity community with excellent examples of authoritative downstream vulnerability context. General feedback to date has been positive, demonstrating that this extra layer of data is something the vulnerability management community may find invaluable for better assessing risk and prioritizing valuable vulnerability management resources. See how to view SADP-enriched CVE Records here.
Looking to Contribute? The CVE SADP Pilot Wants You!

Building directly on this initial momentum, the CVE Program is expanding and extending this pilot to truly maximize its impact. We are widening the scope to invite active participation from CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) across the entire ecosystem as we are looking to increase the number of participating Supplier CNAs, while also seeking more representation from downstream users who consume this information.

To enable the community to thoroughly test the framework and refine data ingestion, we are also extending the overall timeframe of the pilot that was originally scheduled to be completed in July 2026. We are currently mapping out an extension timeline and do not yet have a final end date locked in, but this extended timeframe will help ensure this pilot delivers maximum long-term value.
How to Participate

If you have interest in participating, contact the CVE Program SADP Pilot team using the CVE Request Web Form (choose “General Support”). You can request to be an “active” Supplier CNA participant, an active downstream user/reviewer, or simply request to join our monthly sync meetings to stay up to date on the status of the pilot.

Joining this effort gives community members a direct voice in refining how data is shared globally, while providing downstream users a seat at the table to help reduce confusion and false positives. Even if you do not have the time to participate more materially, you can still make an impact by opening an issue or commenting directly in our SADP GitHub Issues Tracker.
We look forward to hearing from you!

currentNews.title: “CVE in an Era of AI-Enabled Vulnerability Discovery: Opening a Community Discussion” — A Free Virtual Conference

description.altText: CVE Program to host a free public virtual conference, “CVE in an Era of AI-Enabled Vulnerability Discovery,” on July 30, 2026, from 10:00 AM to 2:00 PM EDT (10:00–14:00 UTC).

description.content: The CVE™ Program is opening a structured community discussion about how AI-enabled vulnerability discovery is affecting the CVE Program and the broader vulnerability management ecosystem — and where current models may need to adapt.

We are seeking first-hand observations, discussion topics, and participants to lead and facilitate collaborative conversations across the ecosystem, including researchers, software manufacturers, open source maintainers, bug bounty operators, CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs), Roots, tooling vendors, and downstream CVE data consumers.

description.altText: July 30, 2026 from 1400 to 1800 UTC (10:00 AM to 2:00 PM USA Eastern time)
description.captionText: Registration details are below.

description.content: AI-enabled discovery is affecting more than how vulnerabilities are found. It is also changing how vulnerability information is reported, validated, coordinated, remediated, published, enriched, consumed, and acted upon. The central question is how CVE can continue to serve as a trusted and scalable foundation for vulnerability identification while the broader ecosystem adapts to greater speed, volume, uncertainty, and AI-assisted consumption.

For readers who want more background, the sections below outline several themes that have emerged in CVE Program working group discussions. These themes are intended to help frame the July 30, 2026, forum and invite broader input from the community.
Why AI-Enabled Discovery Matters

Vulnerability discovery and reporting are in a period of significant change. Advances in artificial intelligence are making it easier to identify potential vulnerabilities at greater speed and scale. These capabilities are affecting software development and security research, as well as vulnerability discovery, reporting, and downstream management tasks (such as remediation).

The CVE Program provides a shared identifier system for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities. CVE Identifiers (CVE IDs) give the ecosystem a common language for referring to vulnerabilities across information sources and information workflows. They do not, by themselves, determine an action is required (or what that action is).

These changes matter because CVE information does not move through the ecosystem in isolation. It is created, enriched, correlated, republished, integrated into tools, and ultimately used by defenders to make operational decisions. As AI-enabled discovery accelerates, pressure may increase not only on CVE Record creation, but also on the broader information flows that connect discovery, remediation, publication, enrichment, and downstream action.
Ecosystem Implications

CVE Program working group discussions have focused on five recurring themes: scale, timing, abstraction, chainability, and data quality/correlation. The lifecycle graphic below (click on the image to enlarge it) illustrates how these pressures can appear across discovery, reporting, validation, remediation, CVE Record creation, and downstream use.

description.altText: AI Impacts the Full CVE Lifecycle
description.captionText: Click on image to see enlarged image in new browser window.

description.content: Scale – AI-enabled tools are increasing the volume and velocity of findings, including duplicate and near-duplicate reports. That can make it harder for vendors, maintainers, CNAs, VDP operators, and downstream consumers to identify what reported information is most relevant to them. Higher volume can strain triage capacity, slow remediation, and increase the risk that valid reports are delayed or overlooked. At the same time, AI-enhanced triage may help reduce that burden.

Timing – Traditional vulnerability coordination often assumes that a report can be validated, coordinated, published, enriched, consumed, and acted upon in sequence. AI-enabled discovery is putting pressure on that sequence. Multiple parties may identify the same issue, or related classes of issues, at roughly the same time. In some cases, remediation work, release notes, or other security-relevant update signals from one process may be widely seen while another process has made less progress. Even if each individual sequence executes in the traditional manner, consumers may experience confusion if records, advisories, package updates, databases, and tools do not correlate consistently.

Abstraction – CVE IDs identify vulnerabilities, not every instance of a weakness, test finding, code commit, or analysis artifact. AI-generated reports may increasingly identify “suspicion points”: fragile code patterns, missing defenses, or other signals that suggest security relevance but do not necessarily map cleanly to one confirmed vulnerability. A suspicion point may ultimately correspond to zero, one, or multiple CVE IDs. One challenge is how to encourage useful tracking, root-cause analysis, and remediation guidance when the traditional level of certainty is not yet available.

Chainability – AI-enabled analysis may make it easier to identify how unrelated vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, or not-yet-CVE findings combine into higher-impact attack paths. Consumers may need better ways to understand when an issue that appears lower priority in isolation becomes more significant in context, while preserving the distinction between shared vulnerability information and environment-specific risk decisions.

Data Quality and Correlation – Rapid growth in reporting and CVE Record publication is increasing demand for information that helps consumers assess whether a vulnerability applies to their environment and what action may be appropriate. Consumers need to know where vulnerability information came from, whether it can be trusted, and how it connects to related advisories, fixes, packages, and tools. AI-assisted analysis can help bridge data gaps, but it works best when authoritative sources are clear enough to support reliable correlation across CVE Records, supplier advisories, package updates, vulnerability databases, and tools.
Principles for an Evolving Ecosystem

As the ecosystem evolves, several principles remain stable. The CVE Program will continue to serve as a global public good and shared foundation for vulnerability identification. CVE IDs will remain identifiers, not standalone risk determinations or directives to take specific action. Federation, accountability, transparency, and data quality will remain central to the Program’s operational goals.

At the same time, preserving those principles does not mean preserving every existing assumption about timing, coordination, enrichment, or consumption. AI-enabled discovery may change how quickly information emerges, how completely it can be validated before use, and how consumers connect CVE Records with advisories, package updates, and other ecosystem signals. The Program’s challenge is to preserve a reliable common naming scheme while supporting trusted, useful vulnerability information flows at greater scale and speed.
July 30 Virtual Forum: Who Should Participate, and What Input is Most Useful?

The CVE Program welcomes input from anyone who creates, coordinates, publishes, enriches, consumes or acts on vulnerability information. Community members are encouraged to respond from the perspective most relevant to their work:

• Researchers and bug hunters: How are AI-enabled tools changing what you find, how quickly you find it, how you validate it, and how you report it?
  • Software manufacturers and open source maintainers: How is AI changing internally discovered findings, external reports, triage burden, remediation, CVE Record quality, release practices, and maintainer capacity?
  • VDP and bug bounty operators: How is AI changing submission volume, report quality, duplicate findings, triage workload, and program rules?
  • CNAs and coordination participants: How are AI-enabled reports affecting assignment, disagreements in vulnerability determination, duplicate detection, disclosure timelines, evidence expectations, and publication workflows?
  • TL-Roots and Roots: How are AI-enabled reports affecting CNA community interactions, dispute adjudications, and enforcement of CNA Program Rules?
  • Downstream consumers and tooling providers: How are changes in CVE volume, record quality, uncertainty, roll-up practices, advisories, package updates, and AI-assisted tooling affecting vulnerability management workflows and remediation decisions?

Across all audiences, the Program is especially interested in how vulnerability information moves from discovery to action. In some cases, a supplier may release a security-relevant fix before downstream tools clearly connect that fix to the relevant CVE ID, advisory, scanner result, etc. The Program welcomes examples of how those gaps affect consumer decisions, including whether organizations patch, wait for additional confirmation, miss the signal entirely, or rely on other sources to make a decision.

The Program also welcomes proposed discussion topics on three themes: improving how vulnerability information moves through the ecosystem, representing uncertainty and abstraction more clearly, and helping consumers make reliable remediation and prioritization decisions at greater speed and scale.
Registration Details
This free virtual conference is open to the public. Registration is open until 11:59 PM EDT on July 27, 2026. Register today!

The CVE Program encourages community members to submit proposed discussion topics, session ideas, first-hand observations, and offers to lead or facilitate conversations through the CVE Program GitHub issue tracker: https://github.com/CVEProject/Ideas/issues. Submissions must posted by 5:00 PM EDT on July 9, 2026, to be considered for the agenda.

The July 30, 2026, virtual forum is intended to begin a broader engagement process. The Program expects to route actionable topics to appropriate working groups and governance mechanisms, supplement the forum with additional discussions as needed, and publish a summary of findings and next steps.

currentNews.title: Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records: 259 CNAs on the Enrichment Recognition List for June 1, 2026

description.altText: Increasing the Value of the CVE Record - CNA Enrichment Recognition List

description.content: The “CNA Enrichment Recognition List” for June 1, 2026, is now available with 259 CNAs listed. Published monthly on the CVE website, the list recognizes those CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) that are actively providing enhanced vulnerability data in their CVE Records. CNAs are added to the list if they provide Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) in at least 98% of their records that were published within two weeks of their most recently published record.

CNA Enrichment Recognition List criteria and reporting are intended to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same. Enrichment Recognition List criteria may change over time. The most recent modifications occurred in June 2025 when data pulls were moved from every two weeks and based upon data from the last 12 months, to the current reporting of once-per-month data pulls based upon data from the previous six months.

For more about the recognition list, see “Recognition for CNAs Actively Providing Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records.” To learn more about vulnerability information types like CVSS and CWE, see the CVE Record User Guide. View the most current CNA Enrichment Recognition List on the CVE website Metrics page here.

currentNews.title: CVE Program Report for Quarter 1 Calendar Year (Q1 CY) 2026

description.content: The CVE Program’s quarterly summary of program milestones and metrics for Q1 CY 2026.
Q1 CY 2026 Milestones
Nineteen CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) Added
The nineteen (19) new CNAs added this quarter are listed below under their Top-Level Root (TL-Root) or Root. Scope of coverage is described next to their organization name.
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Industrial Control Systems (ICS) Root:

• CODRA – CODRA’s products and related services. (France)
  • Cribl, Inc. – Vulnerabilities identified in Cribl products, and vulnerabilities discovered by, or reported to, Cribl that are not in another CNA’s scope. (USA)
  • Hackrate Kft. – Vulnerabilities that are discovered, validated, and coordinated through the Hackrate Ethical Hacking Platform, including: software, web applications, APIs, and cloud services; vulnerabilities validated and triaged by our internal security team; and findings disclosed under our coordination that are not in another CNA’s scope. (Hungary)
  • JupiterOne, Inc. – All JupiterOne open source and commercial products. (USA)
  • NIBE Group – Products, services, and solutions developed or sold by NIBE Industrier AB or any of its subsidiaries; open-source projects owned by NIBE Industrier AB or any of its subsidiaries; vulnerabilities in third-party products used by NIBE Industrier AB or any of its subsidiaries which are outside the scope of another CNA; and subsidiaries of NIBE Industrier AB are listed on https://www.nibe.com. (Sweden)
  • Vantive – Vantive’s commercially available products only. (USA)
JPCERT/CC:

• Fujifilm Business Innovation Corp. – Fuji Xerox and FUJIFILM Business Innovation products such as multifunction devices, printers, production printers, software, and cloud services. (Japan)
  • Nintendo Co., Ltd. – System vulnerabilities regarding the Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch Lite, and vulnerabilities regarding Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch applications for which Nintendo is the publisher worldwide. (Japan)
MITRE TL-Root:

• Acer Inc. – Acer issues only. (Taiwan)
  • Bombadil Systems LLC – Vulnerabilities in third-party software discovered by Bombadil Systems that are not in another CNA’s scope. (USA)
  • ByteDance, Ltd. – ByteDance issues only. (China)
  • Canva – All Canva products, including open-source software published and maintained by Canva, as well as vulnerabilities in third-party software discovered by Canva that are not in another CNA’s scope. (Australia)
  • Cygence Pty Ltd – Issues in third-party products identified by, or reported, to Cygence, unless covered by the scope of another CNA. (Australia)
  • DTEX Systems, Inc. – All DTEX products, including DTEX Forwarder for Mac, DTEX Forwarder for Linux, DTEX Forwarder for Windows, and DTEX platform including DTEX Analytics Server. (USA)
  • Project Black – Vulnerabilities discovered by Project Black that are not within another CNA’s scope. (Australia)
  • TCL Electronics Holdings Limited – TCL smart TV, smart pad, and mobile phone devices only. Projects listed on https://github.com/TclSecLab/CNA/blob/main/README_EN.md. (China)
  • Vestel Electronics Industry & Trade Co. – Vestel-owned brands and products only. (Türkiye)
Red Hat Root:

• The HDF Group – All HDF software including HDF5, HDF4, HSDS, HDFView. (USA)
  • Turan Security – Vulnerabilities discovered through independent research conducted by TuranSec to products and projects that are not CNAs themselves. (Uzbekistan)
500+ Organizations Now Participating as CNAs!

As of March 31, 2026, the CVE Program achieved a major milestone of 502 organizations from around the world participating as CNAs in the CVE Program: 499 CNAs and 3 CNAs of Last Resort (CNA-LR). In 2016, the CVE Program (with only 23 CNAs) adopted a strategy to federate the publication of CVE Records by partnering with additional CNAs. Since then, 479 additional organizations (as of the date of this milestone) have partnered with the CVE Program as CNAs and, as a result, the CVE List surpassed the 300,000+ CVE Records milestone in 2025. CNAs are vendor, researcher, open source, CERT, hosted service, bug bounty provider, and consortium organizations authorized by the CVE Program to assign CVE IDs to vulnerabilities and publish CVE Records within their own specific scopes of coverage. Contact information and other partner details for CNAs are available on the List of Partners page.
Ongoing Recognition for CNAs Actively Providing Vulnerability Data Enrichment for CVE Records

The CVE Program publicly recognizes those CNAs that are actively providing enhanced vulnerability data in their CVE Records. The “CNA Enrichment Recognition List,” published monthly, recognizes CNAs that provide Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) information based upon a monthly data pull of the previous six months.

The recognition list was published on January 5 with 263 CNAs recognized, February 2 with 256 CNAs recognized, and March 2 with 256 CNAs recognized.

CNA Enrichment Recognition List criteria and reporting are intended to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same. Enrichment Recognition List criteria may change over time. The most recent modifications occurred in June 2025 when data pulls were moved from every two weeks and based upon data from the last 12 months to the current reporting of once-per-month data pulls based upon data from the previous six months. Future changes to the ERL qualification criteria and reporting may occur over time as the CVE Program continually aims to recognize those CNAs taking on the work to increase the value of CVE Records for downstream consumers, and encourage others to do the same.
CVE Podcast — “CVE Record Disputes Explained”

In this episode of the “We Speak CVE” podcast, MITRE’s CVE™ and CWE™ Project Lead Alec Summers chats with Yves Younan of Cisco, Alex Kreilein of Qualys, Pedro Sampaio of Red Hat, and Anthony Singleton of the MITRE Top-Level Root, about the CVE Record dispute process. Topics include how the dispute policy came to exist and the two types of CVE Record disputes; a walk-through of the process for disputing a CVE Record, including what steps to take and what to expect; why some disputes persist indefinitely; whether all CVE Record disputes need to be resolved; why some disputes remaining visible to the downstream consumer is healthy; an overview of how the CVE Record Dispute Policy was created and how it continues to updated over time; how the CVE Program continuously seeks community input on the dispute process; and more. Read the companion blog article here.
Supplier CNA as Authorized Data Publisher Pilot (SADP Pilot)

In March, the CVE Program announced that it would be conducting a “Supplier CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) as Authorized Data Publisher Pilot (SADP Pilot)” from April 2026 through July 2026 to explore how CVE Records might be made more valuable to the downstream consumer by enabling product suppliers with the ability to publish authoritative product status information directly within CVE Records of upstream vulnerabilities, helping reduce unnecessary investigation and enabling more efficient vulnerability management workflows. Visit the SADP Pilot Repository on GitHub, or read the initial announcement, “Supplier ADP Pilot — CVE Program to Explore Benefits of Supporting VEX-like, Product Status Information in Upstream CVE Records.”
CVE Program Normalizes Formatting of Date/Time Fields Across Historical CVE Records

The CVE Program normalized the formatting of date/time fields across historical CVE Records from February 16-26, 2026. As initially announced on January 6, 2026, the purpose of this maintenance was to update older CVE Records so their date/time values use the same standardized ISO 8601 UTC format already in place for records published or updated since February 2025:
  • yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.sssZ (ISO-8601, UTC)
For example: 2025-07-11T19:32:03.983Z.

In total, this process updated approximately 200,000 historical CVE Records and only effected the formatting of specific date/time string fields (for example, datePublished, dateUpdated, dateReserved, dateRejected, datePublic, dateAssigned, and time values under timeline). The semantic meaning of the dates/times remains the same, and no other parts of the CVE Records were changed. Learn more here.
Community Informed About Agenda and Registration Details for CVE/FIRST VulnCon 2026

In March, the community was informed that the full agenda was now available for CVE/FIRST VulnCon 2026, that was scheduled to be held April 13-16, 2026, at the DoubleTree Resort by Hilton Hotel Paradise Valley – Scottsdale, in Scottsdale, Arizona, USA. Co-hosted by the CVE Program and FIRST, the purpose of VulnCon is to “collaborate with various vulnerability management and cybersecurity professionals to develop forward leaning ideas that can be taken back to individual programs for action to benefit the vulnerability management ecosystem.” In January, the community was informed that registration for both in-person and virtual attendance was now open.
39,080 CVE Records Used as Basis for the “2025 CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses List”

The 2025 CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses list was released by the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) Program on December 11, 2025. The newly released list highlights the most severe and prevalent weaknesses behind the 31,770 CVE Records mapped in the 2024 dataset. The 2025 CWE Top 25 is the second year in a row where the CNA community directly contributed CWE mapping reviews within the dataset, leveraging their expert knowledge of the products and access to information that might not be present in the CVE Record. In general, CNAs are best positioned to provide accurate CWE mapping determinations compared to third-party analysts, as CNAs are the authority for vulnerability information within their CNA scope and those closest to the products themselves. Visit the CWE Top 25 page on the CWE website to view the full 2025 CWE Top 25 List, key insights, methodology, etc.
Q1 CY 2026 Metrics
Metrics for Q1 CY 2026 Published CVE Records and Reserved CVE IDs are included below. Annual metrics are also included in the charts for year-to-year comparisons.

Terminology
  • Published: When a CNA populates the data associated with a CVE ID as a CVE Record, the state of the CVE Record is Published. The associated data must contain an identification number (CVE ID), a prose description, and at least one public reference.
  • Reserved: The initial state for a CVE Record; when the associated CVE ID is Reserved by a CNA.
Published CVE Records

As shown in the table below, CVE Program production was 15,176 CVE Records for Q1 CY 2026. This is a 19% increase from the 12,796 records published in Q4 CY 2025. This includes all CVE Records published by all CNAs and the two CNAs of Last Resort (CNA-LRs).
